title: Why Did You Do That?

source.quote: Eric Berne calculated that in theory there are 72 possible varieties of crossed transaction.

setting: Tuesday evening, a peer-feedback circle in a borrowed conference room. Nadia runs these sessions. A crossed transaction is just a reply that doesn't answer the ego state it was aimed at - and tonight she wants the group to practice spotting the two ways that keeps showing up before everyone goes home.
playAs: Jordan, a member of the peer-feedback circle

L1.line: Read this one with me. Marcus asks Dana, "Did you get a chance to review the budget?" Dana snaps back, "Why is it always my job to review things around here?"
cues: Dana: "always", aggrieved pitch, answers up as if scolded (Child to Parent)
L1.question: What kind of transaction is this?

options.text: Not crossed - they're both just talking about the budget.
options.feedback: Same topic, different vectors: Marcus addressed Dana's Adult and her reply came back from Child, aimed at a Parent he never occupied. That mismatch is exactly what crossed means - staying on-topic doesn't prevent it.

options.text: A crossed transaction - specifically the common shape, an Adult stimulus crossed by a Child-to-Parent response.
options.feedback: Right. Marcus offered Adult-Adult; Dana answered Child-to-Parent instead. Vectors not parallel, and the ego-state he addressed isn't the one that answered.

options.text: A crossed transaction - the rarer shape, where a Parent-pulling stimulus gets answered from Adult.
options.feedback: That's the mirror image of what happened here. Marcus's stimulus was Adult, not Parent or Child, so whatever crossed it has to be a response that didn't answer Adult with Adult - which is the common shape, not the rare one.

L1.lesson: Berne calculated 72 theoretically possible varieties of crossed transaction, but only two show up constantly in practice: an Adult-Adult stimulus crossed by a Child-to-Parent response, or by a Parent-to-Child response. Dana's reply is the first of those two.

L2.intro: "Let's warm up with the common one," Nadia says. "Marcus, give Jordan a plain Adult question. Jordan - answer the way the common crossed shape looks: Adult stimulus, Child-to-Parent response."

beats.line: Jordan, what did you think of the timeline I proposed for the launch?

options.text: Why does it always have to be about your timeline? You never ask what I think until it's already decided.
options.outcome: Nadia nods. "That's it exactly. He offered Adult, you answered Child-to-Parent - 'always', 'never', aimed up at an authority he never claimed. Vectors cross." "Now the rarer one," she says. "Grant's going to pull for your Parent or Child - answer him from Adult and cross him back."
options.lesson: This reproduces the common crossed shape on purpose: Adult stimulus, Child-to-Parent response. The vectors aren't parallel, and the ego-state he addressed (Adult) isn't the one that answered - textbook crossed transaction.

options.text: I think it's solid, maybe a little tight in week two.
options.outcome: "Good answer," Nadia says, "and completely not what I asked for. That's complementary, not crossed - exactly how you'd want to actually answer him, just not tonight's exercise." "Now the rarer one," she adds. "Grant's going to pull for your Parent or Child - answer him from Adult and cross him back."
options.lesson: In real life this is the better move - Adult met with Adult, which is rule 1 (answer the exact state you were addressed in, and it just keeps going), communication continues cleanly. For the specific drill (reproduce a crossed transaction on purpose), it's the wrong target: being the healthiest answer and being the assigned exercise are two different jobs.

options.text: Don't ask me things like that when I haven't even had coffee yet.
options.outcome: "Also crossed," Nadia says, "but the mirror image - Parent down to his Child, not Child up at a Parent. Different shape." "Let's see the rarer one too," she says. "Grant's going to pull for your Parent or Child - answer him from Adult and cross him back."
options.lesson: Both are crossed, but crossed isn't one thing - the two common shapes run in opposite directions (Child-to-Parent vs. Parent-to-Child). Confusing which direction you just produced is confusing which ego state actually got addressed.

beats.line: Honestly, Jordan, I expected you to have caught this review note before it went out. What were you thinking?

options.text: I missed that line. I'll read the review notes out loud before anything ships from now on.
options.outcome: Grant blinks, caught off guard - his Parent-pulling stimulus just got Adult back. "...Right. Make sure of it." Nadia: "There it is. He pulled for your Child, you crossed him into Adult. Rarer, and it's the one that gets used in therapy and at work both."
options.lesson: This reproduces the rarer common shape: a Parent-to-Child stimulus crossed by an Adult-to-Adult response. Crossing is the main tool for getting out of a stuck pattern, not a way of starting a fight - this is what that actually looks like.

options.text: You're right, I'm sorry, I'll be more careful.
options.outcome: "Make sure it doesn't happen again," Grant says, satisfied. Nadia: "And that's the expected complementary answer - Parent down, Child up, same groove continuing. Not wrong to do in real life. Just not tonight's assignment."
options.lesson: This completes his Parent-to-Child stimulus instead of crossing it - perfectly complementary, rule 1, and it leaves the pattern exactly where it was instead of breaking it.

options.text: Maybe if the review process wasn't such a mess, I'd have caught it.
options.outcome: Grant's jaw sets. "So now it's the process's fault?" The room temperature drops. Nadia calls time: "Also crossed - interesting, but that's the common shape again, aimed back at him instead of answering from Adult. Let's reset and try it once more next week."
options.lesson: A rebellious Child reply still lands on the common shape (Child-to-Parent, just defiant instead of compliant) rather than the rarer Adult cross the exercise asked for - and either flavor of Child reply keeps the fight going instead of ending it.

echo.setting: A week later, in a real one-on-one with an actual manager, not a drill.
echo.line: Honestly, I expected more from you on this one.
echo.shape: same two-beat shape as L2, this time for real
